title: E1: dehydrating tert-butanol
subtitle: Acid turns OH into a leaving group; a carbocation loses H⁺

reactants.caption: tert-butanol + sulfuric acid
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group. Use the acid to make a better one.
hintTiers: What would the OH group become if its oxygen took a proton? Would that leave more easily?
The oxygen of the alcohol takes the drawn proton of sulfuric acid; the O–H bond of the acid breaks. Two arrows.
Alcohol oxygen lone pair → the acid's hydrogen; the acid's O–H bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group: the C–OH bond does not break on its own. Protonate the oxygen first so that neutral water can leave.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the alcohol takes the proton. Hydrogen now has two bonds: break the acid's O–H bond onto its oxygen.

oxonium-ion.caption: protonated alcohol (an oxonium ion)
oxonium-ion.learnerPrompt: The oxonium ion has a good leaving group. Let it go.
hintTiers: In E1 the leaving group goes first, on its own. Which bond breaks?
The C–O bond breaks and both electrons go to oxygen: water leaves and a tertiary carbocation forms. One arrow.
The C–O bond → a lone pair on the oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: A concerted E2 needs a strong base. Here the only bases are weak (hydrogen sulfate, water), and the tertiary carbocation is stable enough to form first: water leaves on its own.
Nothing can reach the back of a tertiary carbon: SN2 is impossible here. Let water leave first.

carbocation.caption: tert-butyl cation + water + hydrogen sulfate
carbocation.learnerPrompt: Remove a proton to form the alkene.
hintTiers: A C–H bond next to the positive carbon can donate its electrons to it. What takes the proton?
Hydrogen sulfate takes the drawn hydrogen on a methyl group; that C–H bond becomes the C=C π bond. Two arrows.
Hydrogen sulfate oxygen lone pair → the drawn hydrogen; the C–H bond → a π bond to the cationic carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water adding back to the cation is the reverse of the last step: it happens, but it leads back to the alcohol. Heat drives the elimination: remove a proton.
Hydrogen sulfate is a very weak nucleophile, and any sulfate formed would ionise again. Use it as a base: remove a proton next to the cation.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: those electrons form the π bond. Now the hydrogen needs a base to take it.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The OH group is now OH₂⁺: it can leave as a neutral water molecule, a far better leaving group than hydroxide.
The slow step: the rate depends only on the oxonium ion (unimolecular, the 1 in E1). It works because the tertiary cation is stabilised by three alkyl groups.
The C–H bond next to the empty p orbital gives its electrons to form the π bond. Sulfuric acid is regenerated: it is a catalyst.

mechanismSummary: Sulfuric acid protonates the OH group, turning it into water, a good leaving group. Water leaves on its own, giving the tertiary tert-butyl cation (the slow step). Hydrogen sulfate then removes a proton from a carbon next to the cation, and its C–H electrons form the C=C bond of 2-methylpropene. The acid is given back, so it is a catalyst; heat drives the gaseous alkene off.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 17
